newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian stocks seen toppish with Bel-20 near 2,500.
newsitem.headline: Belgian stocks seen toppish with Bel-20 near 2,500.

text.p: Belgian shares have probably got as good as they can get in 1997, analysts, looking ahead to the rest of the year, say.
Fundamentally and technically, the Belgian bourse is toppish, but could still spring surprises.

"Last December we expected the Bel-20 .BFX to reach 1,980 points by the end of 1997. We are already 20 percent above that," BBL-Vermeulen Raemdonck analyst Thierry Hazevoets said. "At the end of last year no-one predicted the dollar's rise or that bond yields would fall."
The low yields and a 16 percent rise in the dollar against the Belgian franc BEF= have propelled the Bel-20 well beyond even the most optimistic forecasts made at the end of 1996.
Hazevoets now expects the index to end 1997 at around 2,500 points, the same as the average of four other analysts sampled.
The Bel-20 blue chip index ended Thursday at 2,488.07 points, up more than 30 percent on the beginning of the year.

Generale Bank analyst Wim Van Dyke expected the Bel-20 to fall to 2,400 points by the end of September as first-half results due that month from some companies would leave the market disappointed. Chemicals company Solvay was named by several analysts as one such stock.
However, new cash from Bel-20-linked investment products and the anticipation of stronger growth in 1998 should lift the index again by end-December to 2,600 points, Van Dyke said.

"We are going to see new highs in the coming days and then a sell-off which will last into September, when you should buy again," KB Securities analyst Francis Smolders said. The market was technically toppish at around 2,500 points, after which it could correct down by 10 to 15 percent before rising again.
Geert de Mesure, analyst with Bank Delen, expected the Bel-20 to come off its highs, but then stay at lower levels, ending 1997 at around 2,300 points.

"Interest rates will remain low but I don't think the markets will let the dollar stay where it is," De Mesure said. "I can imagine the U.S. (stock) market will begin to feel the impact of the higher dollar on industry and sooner or later the Americans will try to talk (the dollar) down."
Analysts agreed that despite this year's gains there were still bargains to be had.
"There are still some decent shares at relatively cheap prices," Merrill Lynch analyst Nicholas Faes said, citing retailer Colruyt and chemicals and drugs group UCB despite recent strong rises.
He favoured cyclicals, not financials. But financial holding company Almanij could still rise to 21,000 francs. Small caps such as Sipef, Telinfo, Engrais Rosier and Spector offered real potential.
Bruno de Bus of Belgian brokerage Puilaetco recommended UCB, Tessenderlo, Kredietbank, Barco and Ackermans & Van Haaren.

All analysts sampled said the centre of attention over the summer months would be insurer Royale Belge because of rumours it was up for sale. This in turn would help other companies in the Groupe Bruxelles Lambert stable, which includes bank BBL.
De Bus said he would have no problems if Royale Belge rose to 12,000 francs, but some were neutral on the stock.

"Among European insurers, it is the one which has risen most versus its local index this year and there's no other reason for that except speculation. It's too high on a fundamental basis, but you don't get out of a lift which is going up," BBL's Hazevoets said.
He preferred selected cyclicals, such as cement maker CBR, despite recent downgrades by other analysts, oil group PetroFina and steel stocks.
